schools.summary: Keil marks the loose, didactic formula replacing the chronological notice of 2 Kings 18:13; Ellicott gives the name Sin-ahi-iriba and exposes the Chronicler's omission of Hezekiah's tribute to heighten the deliverance.
Henry weighs the providence — the blow fell only after the reformation was established, that God might show himself strong for a reforming people and take the honour of their rescue.
Gill dates the invasion to the fourteenth year, with religion settled, the Philistines beaten, and the Assyrian yoke cast off.
Clarke: God did not disturb the pious prince till the reformation was complete; Wesley reads the emphatic preface — duty may still meet trouble, permitted to try our confidence.

debates.question: Why does the Chronicler omit Hezekiah's tribute and submission to Sennacherib?

sides.position: Because the negotiations had no bearing on the war's after-course
Because the Chronicler was unwilling to record Hezekiah's forced sacrilege
Because his object was to heighten the mighty deliverance, and such details would weaken it

schools.summary: Ellicott renders 'his face was for the war'; Keil explains the covering of the springs — not obstructing but hiding the water by underground channels — and vouches the work from Isaiah 22 and 2 Kings 20:20.
Gill: Hezekiah perceived by the fall of the fenced cities that the enemy meant to storm Jerusalem.
Clarke supplies the tribute the Chronicler suppresses — 300 talents of silver and 30 of gold, the treasuries and temple stripped.
Henry frames the double policy: a cold reception for the country, a warm one for the city.
Keil takes vv.3-5 together: the king showed himself strong and gathered much people to cover the fountains and the brook (the Gihon), reasoning that the Assyrians should find no water.
Gill: Hezekiah consulted nobles and officers how to resist, retard, and distress the enemy.
Wesley draws out the hidden second aim — the water was drawn by secret pipes underground into Jerusalem.
Henry: an army wanting water becomes a heap of dry dust; the very policy of destroying the forage before an invader.
Clarke: without water an army cannot subsist in an arid land, and cites the crusaders of 1099, when the wells were stopped against them.
Ellicott fixes the vocabulary — fountains, wady, the overflow that formed the stream, the rhetorical plural 'kings of Assyria' — and recalls the son of Sirach's memory of the work.
Gill: the people were gathered at the instance of Hezekiah and his officers.
Henry: those who trust God with their safety must yet use proper means, else they tempt him — God will provide, but so must we.

Ellicott unfolds the works — the broken wall, the outer wall of Isaiah 22:11, Millo, the missiles and shields — and lays out the obscure clause over the towers, where Thenius keeps the received reading.
Gill: Hezekiah strengthened himself first of all in the Lord his God, then fortified the city.
Henry: the wall repaired, the towers raised, the darts and shields made — yet those who trust God must still use proper means, or they tempt him.

outliers.note: Lays out a genuine textual crux over 'raised it up to the towers,' preferring 'raised upon it towers,' while noting Thenius keeps the received reading as heightening existing towers.

schools.summary: Keil sets the assembly at the city gate with encouraging words (cf. 2 Chron 30:22); Ellicott fixes 'captains of battles,' a phrase found here only, and the broad open place before the gate.
Gill: captains set over the people to teach the exercises of war and lead the defence.
Clarke: the open places at the gate, where the people came for judgment.
Henry: the undaunted king spoke to the heart of his people, unlike his father Ahaz, whose heart was moved as trees in the wind (Isa. 7:2).

Ellicott traces the charge to Deut. 31:6, Jehoshaphat's word (2 Chron 20:15), and Elisha's assurance (2 Kings 6:16), noting the Chronicler gives substance not exact words; Keil reads 'with us is more' as made precise in v.8.
Clarke: 'more with us than with him' is Elisha's word, soon proved by the angel's slaughter.
Gill: be of good heart and quit yourselves like men.
Henry: the king's first labour was to keep down fear, giving from the prophet the encouragement Isaiah had given from God (Isa. 10:24).

themes: more with us than with him

schools.summary: Ellicott weaves the antithesis from Jer. 17:5, Isa. 31:3, and 1 Sam. 8:20, and reads 'rested themselves upon' as leaning on a staff, and so trusting (Isa. 48:2).
Gill: with Sennacherib only weak, frail, mortal men, nothing in comparison of the Lord.

Henry makes it the king's second labour, the building up of faith: a believing confidence raises us above the fear of man, so that we boldly say, since God is for us, who can be against us (Rom. 8:31).

themes: the LORD to fight our battles
the people leaning on the word

schools.summary: Keil marks the studied brevity beside 2 Kings 18:17-36, with names and place omitted; Ellicott notes a dropped verb, renders 'his power' as dominion, and adduces the Lachish bas-relief in the British Museum.
Gill: the embassy came after Hezekiah had bought the invader off and he had withdrawn.
Clarke: after the tribute Sennacherib withdrew, then sent Rabshakeh with a blasphemous message.
Henry: the impiety and malice of the church's enemies — mean, base artifices to withdraw the people from their king.
Ellicott renders 'why are ye sitting in distress' (cf. Jer. 10:17) and notes the compression of 2 Kings 18:19-25; Keil traces the design to shake trust first in Hezekiah, then in God.
Gill hears the taunt at its widest — on what power in heaven or earth do you trust?
Henry: Satan's own aim, to destroy confidence in God's all-sufficiency, teaching the defenders to say 'there is no help for him in God' (Ps. 3:2).
Ellicott sharpens 'inciting you' and marks the softening of 2 Kings 18:27, adducing Esarhaddon's boast of cutting off food and water; Keil sets it in the calculated loosening of trust.
Gill: the insinuation that surrender is the people's only safety from famine and thirst.
Henry: the reformer painted as one who would betray his subjects to famine and thirst.

themes: faith made to look like folly

schools.summary: Ellicott renders 'before one altar shall ye worship' and notes the Chronicler even more emphatic than Kings on the sole brazen altar; Keil marks the pivot from trust in Hezekiah to trust in God.
Gill bundles the taunt with the three following verses.
Henry: Hezekiah represented as exposing his people to divine displeasure by taking away the high places and altars.

themes: the heathen premise of many altars
the fear of God as supposed cause of ruin

schools.summary: Ellicott notes the Assyrian love of citing predecessors and the dropped list of vanquished states (2 Kings 18:34), adducing Assurbanipal's carrying off of Elam's gods; Keil lays bare the syllogism that reckons the LORD one god among many.
Gill treats the verse within the bundle from v.12.
Henry: Sennacherib boasted of triumphs over the gods of the nations, inferring 'how much less shall your God deliver you?'

themes: what I and my fathers have done

schools.summary: Ellicott glosses 'utterly destroyed' as put under the ban (cf. 2 Kings 18:35); Keil reads the culminating form of the argument — no god of a conquered land had saved his people.
Gill lets the blasphemy speak within the bundle from v.12.
Henry: the false analogy — because Hamath and Arpad's gods failed, the God of Israel must fail — turns boast into blasphemy.

themes: which of the gods could deliver
the affront to the living God
an answer coming from the camp

schools.summary: Ellicott renders 'much less will your gods deliver you' (cf. Isa. 37:10-11), exposes the pagan reckoning of strong nations and strong gods, and notes the singular variant; Keil marks the summing-up of the harangue.
Gill lets the false inference stand exposed by its repetition, closing the bundle.
Henry: the LORD placed beneath all the idols; here the envoys spoke and would write more than they were bidden.

themes: the last boast before the answer

schools.summary: Ellicott: the verse shows the report is not full, and renders 'against Jehovah the true God' (cf. Isa. 37:23); Keil sets the servants' speech in the march toward deliverance.
Gill: they said more than is here recorded, as in Kings and Isaiah.
Henry: the servants, learning insolence from their master, spoke more than he bade; God resents what is said against his servants as against himself.

themes: the LORD and his servant together

schools.summary: Ellicott renders 'letters wrote he to reproach,' untangles the chronology (the letter followed the Tartan's mission, 2 Kings 19:8-14), and marks the parenthesis and the Chronicler's abbreviation; Keil the single thread of the taunt.
Gill refers to the fuller record in Kings.
Clarke points to 2 Kings 19:9, 14.
Henry: to rail in writing, being more deliberate, is so much the worse.

themes: the written charge before the LORD

schools.summary: Ellicott notes the LXX/Vulg singular 'he cried' (the Rabshakeh) and the purpose of terror, the rare verb 'to affright' (Neh. 6:9); Keil the reaching past the ambassadors to the people.
Gill: the messengers cried in the Jews' speech, though asked to use the Syrian tongue.
Henry: the shout meant to frighten the people from their hope in God (Ps. 71:11), taking the city by weakening the defenders' hands.

themes: a people forearmed by their king

schools.summary: Ellicott: the Chronicler dwells on this blasphemy as the cause of the overthrow, tracing 'the work of the hands of man' to Hezekiah's prayer (2 Kings 19:18).
Gill names the God dishonoured — the only living and true God, worshipped in the temple.
Henry: 'the God of Jerusalem,' compared with the dunghill gods, as if an eternal Spirit had no more power than a stone or stock of a tree.
Ellicott renders 'upon this,' ties the cry to Hezekiah's prayer (2 Kings 19:16) and the nobles sent to Isaiah (2 Kings 19:2-4), and compares 'cried to heaven' with 2 Chron 30:27.
Gill: Isaiah beyond doubt prayed too, since he received a message from the LORD to send the king.
Henry: the duty of the church's friends in distress is to pray and cry to heaven; a happy time when king and prophet join in prayer.

themes: the king and the prophet pray
the true weapon of the city
the answer to be an angel

schools.summary: Keil: the whole host annihilated, the king slain by his sons; Ellicott supplies the 185,000 of 2 Kings 19:35, renders 'he hid,' and names Adrammelech and Sharezer, whom the Chronicler leaves nameless.
Gill weighs the options — Gabriel (Targum), the pestilence (Josephus), a pestilential wind — but insists it was of God, however effected.
Wesley follows the Targum — Gabriel, with lightning, in the passover night; Clarke names the parricides and the god Nisroch.
Henry: the sword of an angel triumphing over the mighty men, then the king cut off by his own sons — mortified first, then murdered.

debates.question: By what means did the angel destroy the Assyrian host?

sides.position: By an angelic agent — the Word sending Gabriel, with fire, in the passover night
By a pestilence or a hot pestilential wind (natural means)
By an angel of the LORD, the means left unspecified but wholly of God

outliers.note: Reports Hitzig's view of a 'great natural miracle' and the conjecture that Isaiah composed Psalms 46-48 to commemorate the deliverance.

themes: the king slain by his sons

schools.summary: Ellicott marks the Chronicler's own comment (cf. 2 Kings 18:7), would add 'his enemies,' and emends 'guided them' to 'gave them rest round about' with the LXX and Vulgate; Keil defends the received text — 'he protected them round about.'
Gill: no stroke was struck but by the LORD.
Henry: he guided, that is, guarded them on every side; God defends his people by directing them.

debates.question: How should the closing phrase 'and guided them on every side' be read?

sides.position: Keep the received text: 'he protected/led them round about'
Emend to 'and gave them rest round about,' with the LXX and Vulgate

schools.summary: Keil takes the 'many' chiefly of neighbouring peoples freed from the enemy; Ellicott names the minchah, the envoys of Merodach-baladan (2 Kings 20:12) and the Philistines, and renders 'lifted up to the eyes of all the nations.'
Gill: nations convinced the deliverance was by the LORD alone brought their offerings to the temple.
Clarke: they saw Jehovah was the protector of the land and would not have such a man for an enemy.
Henry: strangers supplicated God's favour, enemies deprecated his wrath, and both brought gifts; by God's favour enemies are lost and friends gained.

themes: gifts to the LORD and to Hezekiah
honour that would prove a trial

schools.summary: Ellicott: this single verse epitomises 2 Kings 20:1-11 and Isaiah 38, the sign being the shadow on the dial of Ahaz; Keil notes the Chronicle gives only hints, God answering through the prophet.
Gill defers to the fuller narrative in Kings.
Clarke likewise sends the reader to 2 Kings 20.
Henry frames the three heads of the reign's close — sickness and recovery, sin and repentance, honour living and dead — and names the sign, the sun's going back ten degrees.

Keil locates the pride in the display of treasures to the Babylonian embassy (2 Kings 20:12-15) and the wrath foretold (2 Kings 20:16-18); Ellicott adds that Judah and Jerusalem shared the guilty confidence in an arm of flesh.
Clarke: a vain confidence and pleasure in riches; Wesley traces the swelling to the victory, the recovery, and the Babylonian embassy, as if done for his own virtue.
Gill reads 'the benefit' of both deliverances, from Assyria and from sickness.
Henry: when he had destroyed other idolatries he began to idolize himself, making God's favours the fuel of his pride.
Ellicott finds the humbling in the king's 'Good is the word of the LORD' (2 Kings 20:19); Keil: the judgment postponed, breaking only later in the Chaldean invasion.
Gill supposes sackcloth, fasting, prayer, and confession.
Clarke: he grew sorry, deprecated the wrath, and the displeasure was turned away.
Henry draws the rules of a repented heart-sin, and notes the people humbling themselves with their king.

themes: the people mourning with the king

schools.summary: Keil ranks Hezekiah with David, Solomon, and Jehoshaphat, and the treasure-chambers with the 'house of precious things' of 2 Kings 20:13; Ellicott renders 'all vessels of desire' and takes the shields for arms in general.
Gill traces the riches to the Assyrian spoil and the nations' gifts.
Clarke glosses keley chemdah, desirable vessels or utensils.
Henry reads the inventory as the honour providence did the king, for God had given him very much substance.

Keil describes the magazines and stalls, like David (1 Chron 27:25) and Uzziah (2 Chron 26:10), with the transposed Hebrew words; Ellicott adds the Egyptian store-cities (Exod. 1:11) and the copyist's transposed clause 'flocks for folds.'
Gill takes the corn, wine, and oil for the produce of the king's own fields under officers, as David's.

Keil argues the word cannot mean ordinary cities but watch-towers or folds (cf. 2 Kings 17:9); Ellicott renders 'watch-towers' for the flocks and herds (Isa. 1:8; 2 Chron 26:10), and 'substance' as wealth in cattle.
Gill keeps 'cities' with storehouses and dwellings for the herdsmen, noting the Vulgate's 'six cities.'
Wesley: towns repaired, fortified, and beautified for the kingdom's honour and safety.
Henry reads the closing clause as the ground of all — God had given him very much substance.

debates.question: What did Hezekiah 'provide himself' — cities or watch-towers?

sides.position: Watch-towers or folds for the protection of flocks and herds

themes: a catalogue turned to a hymn

schools.summary: Keil explains the covered upper outlet of Gihon brought westward by a subterranean channel into the city of David; Ellicott confirms it from 2 Kings 20:20, where the pool and conduit close Hezekiah's history.
Gill cites Procopius (Gihon as Siloam) and Maundrell's measurement of the pool.
Clarke: canals from the west side to the city of David; Wesley describes the upper and lower pools (Isa. 7:3; 22:9) and the diverting of the stream by pipes.
Henry ties the work to the war (vv.3-4): the water gathered into a new place for the city's convenience, and the king prospered in his good works.

outliers.note: Records the old identification of Gihon with Siloam (from Procopius) and Maundrell's eyewitness measurement of the pool.

themes: he prospered in all his works

schools.summary: Ellicott: the 'wonder' is the sign of v.24, an inquiry fitting for Babylon the home of divination; Keil fixes 'and accordingly,' God permitting the sin to try and humble the king; both read 'to try' as 'to tempt.'
Gill: they came to inquire of the sun's going back, setting aside the Targum's tables and Grotius's Assyrian overthrow.
Wesley: God left him to himself and suffered Satan to try him, that he might know his infirmities; the wonder either the sun or the Assyrians' fall.
Henry: God left him to himself to be proud of his wealth, to keep him from being proud of his holiness.

debates.question: What did the Babylonian envoys come to inquire about?

sides.position: The astronomical wonder — the sun's or shadow's going back
The destruction of the Assyrian army
The two tables of stone in the ark

themes: God left him to try him

schools.summary: Keil reads 'goodness' as pious deeds (2 Chron 6:42) and the 'vision of Isaiah' as the prophet's book; Ellicott would omit the 'and,' making the vision a section of the book of the kings, an authority beyond the canonical Kings.
Gill glosses the goodness as acts of piety and liberality.
Clarke points to Isaiah's own chapters (Isa. 36-39).
Henry: that Isaiah wrote his life is part of the king's honour, recorded for an example.

Ellicott renders 'the ascent' and infers the old royal sepulchres were full (Manasseh, Amon, Josiah likewise not laid there); Keil: buried on the height of the graves, with a great burning of spices as for Asa.
Gill: he slept with his fathers, the settled idiom for death.
Clarke reads 'the chiefest' as the respect paid to the best of their kings since David.
Henry: as great a burning as for Asa, and lamentation as for Josiah; a debt owed to those eminently useful, to honour them at their death.

debates.question: What does 'the chiefest of the sepulchres' signify?

sides.position: The most honourable place, among the chief of the kings
'The ascent' / a grave on higher ground, the old royal tombs being full
